- [x] **Enforce migration numbering with a check, not prose.** Raised 2026-09-22 after two in-flight branches both shipped `0069` (`0069_seed_standard_diet.sql` on the diet branch and `0069_assistant_actions.sql` on `claude/assistant-v1-schema`) and both were applied to dev before anyone noticed — the same clash as the two `0067` PRs earlier. CLAUDE.md already says the next number is one past the highest on `main` and that only one in-flight branch may carry a migration, but it is prose that nothing enforces, and `apply-migrations.mjs --status` reports `0 pending` while dev holds rows main has no file for, so the divergence is invisible. Add a check that fails at commit time (`.githooks/pre-commit`) and in CI: a new file under `supabase/migrations/` must be numbered exactly one past the highest on `origin/main`, and no two files may share a number. Worth pairing with a `--drift` mode on `apply-migrations.mjs` that lists rows in `schema_migrations` with no matching file — dev currently has **two**, not three: `--status` reported 72 applied against 70 files on `main` with `0 pending` (checked 2026-09-23), so exactly two recorded rows have no file. They are the two renumberings — `0067_public_resident_cards.sql` (now `0068`) and `0069_assistant_actions.sql` (now `0070`, commit `34bf49e`). `0069_seed_standard_diet.sql` kept its number and is still a file on `main`, so it is not an orphan. Both leftovers are harmless, but note that the count in this item was wrong until someone did the arithmetic by hand — which is the whole argument for the flag: an orphan count nobody can read off a command is an orphan count that drifts in the notes as well as the database.

- [x] **Make production drift visible: nothing records what production has actually run.** Raised 2026-09-22, alongside the numbering item above and arguably the larger half of it. `schema_migrations` lives inside each database, so the repo has no idea what production has applied and `apply-migrations.mjs --status` only ever answers for the database it is pointed at. `0069_seed_standard_diet.sql` was applied to **production** while `main` had no file for it at all, and sat that way until PR #46 merged; dev meanwhile held three rows with no file on `main`, and `--status` cheerfully reported `0 pending` throughout. Drift is silent in both directions and nobody finds out until someone rebuilds a database or renumbers a file. Note the only thing that prevented a second production apply was accidental: `scripts/worktree.mjs new` copies `.env.local` but not `.env.deploy.production`, so a feature worktree physically cannot reach production — while the main checkout has the file and can. That is luck, not design. Worth: a `--drift` mode that diffs `schema_migrations` against the files on `origin/main` for a named environment and names both halves (applied-but-missing, present-but-unapplied); a `--status` that says which files on `origin/main` production has **not** run, so the pre-deploy gap is one command; and a loud refusal (or at least a prompt) when `--env production` is used from a branch whose migration is not yet on `origin/main`, since schema is supposed to reach `main` before any database. See `docs/decisions.md` 2026-09-22 for the 0069 clash this came out of.

- [x] **`deploy.mjs` ships code without ever asking whether the database has the schema it needs.** Raised 2026-09-30 after it went wrong twice in one day. `deploy.mjs` guards a lot before it builds — branch is `main`, working tree clean, `main` level with `origin/main`, `package.json` matching `latestRelease`, `unreleased` empty — and then deploys without checking a single migration. `apply-migrations.mjs --drift <env>` answers exactly that question and already shares its implementation with Settings → System status (`src/lib/migration-drift.ts`), so the work is wiring, not building. **Two consecutive releases, both on 2026-09-30, and the difference between them was luck rather than process:** on `0.10.0` the deploy was started before `0113`–`0116` were applied, and got away with it only because a deploy spends its first minutes building — the migrations were applied alongside it and reached `No drift` at 116 files while the deploy was 134 seconds in and still compiling, so the schema landed before the Worker upload. It was noticed only because an unrelated `--drift` could not write to `deploy.log` (`Device or resource busy`). On `0.10.1` the luck ran out: `0117` went on about an hour *after* the release was live, and its consumer had shipped in that release (`17c7f0d`, the Microchipped tick on `/adopt/[id]`, with `src/app/adopt/[id]/page.tsx` and `src/lib/residents/public.ts` both selecting `is_microchipped`), so the **public adoption profile was querying a column that did not exist**. How long that lasted cannot be established, because that deploy was run without `>> deploy.log` and its start time is unrecorded. Both are written up in `docs/releases/2026-09-30.md`. **What to build:** in the `GUARDED` block (`uat` and `production` only — leave `test` alone, where running ahead is normal and wanted), refuse the deploy when the target database is missing any migration, listing the pending filenames and the `apply-migrations.mjs` command to fix it, and exit `2` like the sibling guards. **Get the comparison right, because the obvious one is wrong:** the rule is *every migration file in the commit being deployed must be applied to the target*, **not** "the target matches `origin/main`". Extra applied rows are fine — schema ahead of code is the safe direction this project deliberately uses, and a migration belonging to the *next* release can legitimately sit on `main` already. `0118` was in exactly that position during `0.10.1`: on `main`, belonging to `#236` which merged after the cut, and correctly not applied. A naive equality check would have refused that deploy for a file it did not need. In practice the two formulations coincide, because the existing guard already requires `HEAD` to equal `origin/main` — but they should not be *written* as the same thing, or the check breaks the first time someone deploys a tag or a hotfix. **And distinguish "the database says it is behind" from "could not ask":** refuse on the first, warn loudly and continue on the second. A deploy already depends on the network, so this is not the `release-prs.mjs` situation where failing closed on a blip was the thing to avoid; but a Supabase timeout should not be able to block a release either. Worth pairing with the reverse check at the other end: `apply-migrations.mjs` could warn when it applies a file whose consumer is not yet deployed, which is the same information read the other way round.

- [x] **Every guard on the deploy is on the copy nobody is served by.** Raised 2026-10-01, and it is the sibling of the item above: that one is now done, which is exactly what makes this one visible. `deploy.mjs` refuses a `uat`/`production` deploy unless the branch is `main`, the tree is clean, `main` is level with `origin/main`, `package.json` matches `latestRelease`, `unreleased` is empty — "ships only a written-down release" — and, since the item above, unless the target database holds every migration the commit carries. **`scripts/pi/deploy-pi.sh` has none of that.** It is 51 lines: `git fetch origin main` → `git checkout main` → `git reset --hard origin/main` → `npm ci` → `npm run build` → `systemctl restart`. It does run `apply-migrations.mjs --status | tail -1`, but only *prints* it, with a comment saying a build against a database missing a migration is still a valid build — which was a reasonable position before `deploy.mjs` started refusing in that exact case, and is now an asymmetry rather than a decision. **And the Pi is the copy that serves users**: `ORIGIN_HOST` is `pi.lannacare.org` in the production block, and `lannacare.org` answers `x-lanna-served-by: pi`. The Worker is the fallback. So the whole release discipline — cut, record, version, schema check — is enforced on the path that answers only when the Pi times out. **What it costs, all three observed rather than theorised:** (a) **code reaches users without a release cut.** Every note in `0.11.0` was already live before it was cut, because the Pi had been reset to `origin/main` by earlier deploys; release notes now describe what people already have, and `/releases` can show an older version than the app's behaviour. (b) **The release-time gate never runs for it.** `docs/release-smoke-test.md`'s "every PR in this release has a completed test plan — check this by hand" is a pre-*deploy* step, and there is no deploy step here to hang it on. (c) **`npx wrangler rollback --env production` is no longer the production rollback.** It reverts the Worker, which is not serving. Rolling the Pi back means `git reset --hard <sha>` and a rebuild, and that is written down nowhere as a rollback path — while four release records in `docs/releases/` state the `wrangler rollback` position as though it were the whole answer. That documentation is wrong from 2026-09-30 onward and should be corrected with this item. **What to build:** the cheap version is to make `deploy-pi.sh` run the same two checks `deploy.mjs` already has, reusing them rather than restating them — `unreleased` empty and `package.json` matching `latestRelease` for a production or uat deploy, and `missingFromDatabase(deployedMigrations(git), applied)` for the schema, refusing with the same messages and keeping "could not ask" a warning. A `--force` for a genuine emergency is fine *if* it prints loudly and the reason ends up in a record; the sign-in outage of 30 September is exactly the case for one, and it was handled properly through a PR anyway. Keep `--env test` unguarded, as `deploy.mjs` does. **The harder question to settle first, because the fix depends on it:** is the Pi meant to be continuously deployed from `main`, or to be a release target like the Worker? If continuous deployment is wanted — and it has its merits, since it is how the 30 September fix reached users fast — then the honest change is the opposite one: stop pretending a cut release gates production, say so in `docs/release-smoke-test.md`, and move the test-plan gate to merge time where it would actually bite. What cannot hold is the present state, where the documents describe a gate that the serving path does not have. Worth pairing with a version endpoint served by the app rather than the Worker: `/api/releases/current` is answered by `worker/index.mjs:158` before the origin is consulted, so there is currently **no way to ask what the Pi is running** without signing in — the `0.11.0` record could only state it by quoting a terminal someone pasted into chat.

- [x] **A `.env.*.local` for the wrong environment silently bakes that environment's host into the build, and nothing can see it.** Found 2026-10-01 by Lutan: Google sign-in on `test.lannacare.org` returned him to `http://localhost:3000`. **The chain, proven rather than inferred:** `.env.production.local` existed on the dev machine — generated by `scripts/pi/write-env.mjs` for the *production* environment, header and all, presumably left from the Pi setup — and it sets `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://lannacare.org`. `next build` is always a production build, so Next loads `.env.production.local` for **every** deploy including `deploy:test`. `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values are inlined into the compiled output at build time, so the test build carried `https://lannacare.org` in **24 places across 19 files**. On test, `getSiteOrigin()` therefore returned the production host, `signInWithGoogle` sent `redirectTo=https://lannacare.org/auth/callback`, the **dev** Supabase project rejected it as off-allow-list, and Supabase fell back to that project's Site URL — `http://localhost:3000`. Moving the file out of the repo and redeploying fixed it: `strip-baked-env` went from 12 vars to 10, and the inlined host went from 24 occurrences to 0. **Three things made it invisible, which is the real point.** (a) The file is gitignored (`.env.*.local`), so it appears in no diff and no review. (b) `strip-baked-env` is the mechanism that exists to stop dev values shipping, and it **cannot** help here — its own header says "NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are inlined by `next build` separately and don't depend on this file", because it only empties `.open-next/cloudflare/next-env.mjs`. (c) The only visible symptom in the deploy output was the var count going from 10 to 12, which means nothing unless someone knows what it was yesterday. **And it is worse in the other direction than the one we hit.** Here a production host leaked into test, which breaks sign-in loudly. Run `write-env.mjs --env test` on this machine once and the *next production deploy* bakes `https://test.lannacare.org` into production — where `getSiteOrigin()` would then hand the test host to OAuth redirects, `metadataBase`, and anything else that asks for the site origin, on the real site, with no error anywhere. **Two fixes, and the second is the better one:** (a) make `deploy.mjs` refuse when a `.env.*.local` naming a different environment is present, printing the filename — cheap, and it sits beside the check already there that refuses when the Supabase project does not match the target (`appEnvForSupabaseUrl`, which is the same class of mistake caught one layer down); (b) stop relying on env-file precedence at all and have the deploy set `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` explicitly for the environment being built, so there is nothing to leak and no file ordering to reason about. (b) also fixes the case where the file is absent: today an absent value falls back to the request host, which is right for the Worker and wrong for the Pi, and that distinction is currently carried by a generated file rather than by the deploy. Either way, also worth asking why `write-env.mjs` — documented as a Pi script — had been run on the dev machine, and whether it should refuse to write outside the Pi.




- [x] **A release's PR list is built from `git log --first-parent`, which cannot see every PR.** Found 2026-09-29 preparing `0.9.1`. #213 (`claude/stock-edit-history`, which brought migration `0112`) reached `main` through a plain `Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin/main'` rather than a merge commit naming the PR, so it does **not** appear in `git log --oneline --first-parent <last-release>..HEAD` — the listing every cut plan and every release record uses to enumerate a release's PRs. It was found only by tracing `0112`'s author commit back to its branch, and the release was nearly recorded as eight PRs rather than nine. **Nothing was lost this time**: #213's test plan existed and its release-notes line was a sound `n/a: a shelter user sees no change; the history it now feeds is not shown anywhere`. The failure mode is what matters — a PR the audit cannot see is a PR whose test plan nobody checks and whose *missing* release note nobody notices. Note which gate this defeats: `docs/release-smoke-test.md`'s pre-deploy item is "Every PR in this release has a completed `docs/test-plans/<feature>.md` — **check this by hand**", explicitly by hand because `test-plan` reports red without blocking a merge. A hand check against an incomplete list passes silently, which is worse than no check, because it produces a tick. **How it happens:** any route by which a PR's commits join `main`'s first-parent line without their own merge commit — a branch that merges `origin/main` into itself and is then fast-forwarded, a squash or rebase merge, or a second branch that carried the first one's commits along with it. So it is not a one-off mistake to be avoided by discipline; it is a property of the merge shape, and three of the four shapes are ones GitHub offers by default. **Fix options:** (a) enumerate from GitHub rather than git — `gh pr list --state merged` filtered to PRs whose merge commit is an ancestor of `HEAD` but not of the previous release's SHA; authoritative, but needs network and `gh` auth; (b) drop `--first-parent` and read every commit in the range, grouping by branch name from the merge subjects; catches more, but lists nothing for a branch whose name is gone; (c) **cross-check against the two artifacts every feature must have** — for each file added under `supabase/migrations/` and each `docs/test-plans/*.md` in the range, assert its introducing PR is in the list. This is the cheap safety net and it would have caught this exact case: `0112` was in the range with no PR in the list; (d) a `scripts/release-prs.mjs <since-sha>` doing (a) with (b) as fallback and (c) as an assertion, printing the list a cut plan pastes and exiting non-zero when they disagree. (c) alone is worth having even without the rest, since it needs no network and no new syntax. Worth doing before the next release rather than after: the by-hand check is the only thing standing between an unverified feature and production, and it has now been shown to be checkable against the wrong list.




- [x] **The photo proxy serves any known Drive file to a signed-out visitor, internal attachments included.** Found 2026-09-25 while closing anon's function EXECUTE (`0082`, see `docs/decisions.md`, "Anon loses the functions"). `/api/photos/<fileId>` asks `is_known_drive_file`, which says yes for *every* `attachments` row (blood-test and procedure files, not just resident photos), `project_photos`, `maintenance_photos`, the site photos and Shelter Friend logos, and then streams the bytes with no session check. The only barrier is that a Drive file id is hard to guess; anon cannot list them, but an id that leaks (a shared link, a screenshot of a URL, browser history on a shared shelter PC) opens that file to anyone. And the edge cache (`caches.default`) is keyed by URL alone, so a file a signed-in user viewed is served from cache to anyone with the URL for 24h whatever the database says. Decide what the public side needs: probably the files behind `public_resident_photos`, `public_project_photos`, `site_content(_photos)` and `public_shelter_friends` logos. Then either split the check (`is_public_drive_file` for anon, the current one for signed-in users) or require a session for anything else, and make the cache key or `Cache-Control` distinguish the two (`private` for non-public files). Not a schema-only PR: the route changes with it.
- [x] **Take `is_known_drive_file` back from anon.** Since `claude/photo-proxy-session-check` the photo proxy asks `is_public_drive_file`, and for anything else the caller's own RLS on `attachments`, `project_photos`, `maintenance_photos` and `shelter_friends`; nothing anon-facing calls `is_known_drive_file` any more. `0082` still grants anon EXECUTE on it, and it answers yes for any internal file id, so a signed-out caller can confirm that an internal file exists. A small schema PR: revoke from anon (and probably authenticated: the app no longer calls it), and move it out of `check-public-views.mjs`'s allow-list in the same PR, or that check fails. `check-shelter-friends.mjs` and `check-public-drive-file.mjs` call it as the owner and should be unaffected. **Only after the route change is deployed to production**: until then production's proxy still calls it as anon, and revoking would break every public photo.

- [ ] **Roles and permissions each shelter configures: a matrix of activities × roles in Settings, and roles defined at setup — design first.** Lutan, 2026-10-03, thinking about multi-tenancy. Shelters are organised differently: one has a staff member who handles purchasing, another leaves that to Management. Today's roles are a fixed enum (`admin`, `management`, `staff`, `vet`, `volunteer`, `public_viewer`) with their rights hard-coded in about a dozen app predicates (`isShelterRole`, `canManage`, `canStocktake`, `canRecordDelivery`, `canArchiveMedical`, `canWriteMaintenance`, `canWriteProjects`, `canDoJob`, `canUseAssistant`, …) and in RLS across roughly 26 migrations. That cannot vary per shelter. **What is wanted:** (1) **A catalogue of activities with no grey areas.** Every action in the system is one named activity, each set per role to **Edit / Read / None** (or **Yes / No** where reading makes no sense, e.g. "record a death"). Where one screen hides two different powers (create vs delete, record vs approve, see a contact's name vs their phone), split it into two activities rather than adding levels, so every cell means exactly one thing. (2) **A matrix in Settings:** activities down the side, the shelter's roles across the top, admin-editable. (3) **Roles defined per shelter at setup:** a shelter can add a role ("Purchasing", "Senior Staff", "Kennel lead") and set its column, or keep the defaults. **Design points to settle in the paper:** (a) **Defaults reproduce today exactly.** Ship the six current roles as the starting template, filled in so that switching to the matrix changes nothing for Lanna, proved by a check that compares each default cell with today's behaviour. (b) **Some things are not configurable.** Admin always has everything and cannot be edited away; no change may leave a shelter with no one able to edit the matrix; Settings → Security keeps its 2-step rule; `public_viewer` and signed-out visitors stay fixed. (c) **Data scope is separate from capability.** A vet seeing only their clinic's residents (0108) is a *scope*, not a cell, so model scopes apart (or as a small fixed set of scope options per role) rather than forcing them into Edit/Read/None. (d) **Enforcement must be in the database, not only the menu.** One SQL function such as `has_permission('stock.delivery', 'edit')` used by every policy and `security definer` guard, and one `can()` in TypeScript replacing the predicates, both reading the same tables. Decide how it stays fast under RLS (a `stable` function over a small cached table, or the role's permissions placed in the JWT by Supabase's custom access token hook, which means a change applies at the next token refresh — say so in the UI). (e) **Everything that keys on a role name today** has to move to activities: the manual's and `/releases`' per-role filtering (`isForRole`, topic `roles`), recurring-job eligibility, the assistant, nav and route guards, the role walkthrough. (f) **Changes are audited** (who changed which cell, when) through `audit_log` (0121), and the matrix can be exported, since it is also what a shelter's acceptance sign-off is checked against. **Define the catalogue once:** the role-by-activity acceptance matrix (Documentation) needs the same list of activities, so it should be generated from this catalogue rather than kept as a second list. **Where it sits:** it is part of the multi-shelter work (the spike just below): `roles` and the matrix are per `shelter_id` once tenancy lands, but the catalogue and enforcement can be built for one shelter first, and it is cheaper before seven shelters' data exists than after. **[STRUCK 2026-10-19: the Senior Staff item is closed — Lutan: *"Senior staff is not a thing … any question about what a role should be able to do is not applicable as it’s configurable in the system."* There is no ordering question left to settle, and nothing here waits on one.]** **What the cards model already settles for Lanna, so this item does not re-ask it:** what a role may do is data today, set by giving the role cards on Settings → Who does what (`0194`). **What is genuinely left to this item is the per-shelter half**: a catalogue and a matrix that *each shelter* configures at setup, keyed on `shelter_id` once tenancy lands — not "what should a role be able to do", which is answered. **Deliverable:** `docs/roles-and-permissions.md` with the full activity catalogue (every page and action, from the manual's topics and the current predicates and policies), the default matrix, the non-configurable rules, the data model (`roles`, `role_permissions`, `user_roles.role_id`, tenancy columns), the enforcement and caching choice and a migration path from the enum. Agree it with Lutan, record it in `docs/decisions/`, then schema PRs and the build in stages: catalogue and enforcement first, behaviour unchanged; then the Settings matrix; then custom roles. **Note 2026-10-09 (`remove-staff-role`):** the default template is now five live roles, not six: Staff is archived (`0173`), so (a)'s "six current roles" reads Admin, Management, Doctor, Volunteer and Public viewer, plus Lanna's configured 2IC, Head of Maintenance and Head of Medical. Nothing else in this item is closed by that. **Note 2026-10-10:** stage 2, the Settings grid, is pulled forward as its own item at the top of Next up (*Settings → Who does what*), at Lutan's request; this item keeps stage 3, roles a shelter adds. **Note 2026-10-11 (`perm-drop-enum`, `0181`):** what this item names as the problem is gone: `user_roles.role`, `legacy_role`, `current_user_role()` and the `app_role` type were dropped, so a role is only ever a row in `roles` and no function, view or line of app code names one as a string. Stage 3 (roles a shelter adds at setup) is the part still open.
  **Status 2026-10-11 (updated by `who-does-what-edit`): stage 2 is built: an Admin edits the matrix on the grid page, behind 2-step, with prerequisite rules and every change in Recent changes. Stage 3 (roles a shelter adds) is not started, so this item stays open. Earlier status: stage 2's screen exists, view only** (`who-does-what-view`): Settings → Who does what shows the matrix, with every box the system does not yet obey marked. Not ticked: editing it is `who-does-what-edit`, and stage 3 (roles a shelter adds) is not started. See the *PRIORITY: Settings → Who does what* item at the top of Next up.

- [x] **Spike: can the app hold several shelters in one database? Measure it, do not estimate it.** **DONE 2026-10-09 (`claude/multi-tenancy-spike`; no schema merged): `docs/decisions/2026-10-09-multi-tenancy-spike.md`.** Measured on dev in a rolled-back harness: one restrictive policy per table holds for all 63 tenant tables, but **all 13 `public_*` views are owner-run and 9 leaked a second shelter to anon**, 17 staff views leaked, and a Lanna admin wrote another shelter's microchip through a definer RPC. Fix tested: re-own the 38 views and 58 definer functions to a role without `BYPASSRLS` → 0 anon leaks, cross-tenant writes refused, no change for Lanna. **Build ≈ 50 h (40–65)**, plus a catalogue lint and a permanent canary diff as the answer to "how would we know". All 10 Cooper `.org` names still free on 2026-10-09; Lutan to choose. Original item: Lutan, 2026-09-28: seven shelters have shown interest — five in Chiang Mai, two elsewhere in Thailand — and the system would be **a gift to all of them**, so the ongoing cost must be as close to zero as possible (Lutan carries his own time and Claude costs, the shelters carry their own domains). **That constraint decides the architecture.** A silo (one Supabase project per shelter) cannot meet it: the free tier allows two projects per organisation and pauses a project after a week idle, so seven shelters means seven paid projects, forever, for a gift. Pooling — one database, a `shelter_id` on every table — keeps the marginal cost of each shelter at zero, because it adds no new services: the same two projects, the same Worker, the same Pi origin, the same weekly backup. **So the decision is effectively made; what is not known is the cost of getting there, and that is what this item buys.** Do it on a throwaway branch and do not merge it: add `shelter_id`, a `current_user_shelter_id()` helper (shaped like `current_user_vet_id()` from `0102`), and tenancy as **restrictive** policies — the pattern `0100` already uses for the `aal2` check on `user_roles`, where an `as restrictive` policy is AND-ed with every existing permissive one. That means roughly **one restrictive policy per table (~45), not a rewrite of all 181**. Then push it through the parts restrictive policies do not save you: **53 `security definer` functions**, which bypass RLS by design and each need their own tenant check, and **58 views**. Report a real number of hours and a list of the places that fought back. **Design the spike around the anonymous tier specifically** — the `public_*` views are served to signed-out visitors, so a tenancy miss there publishes another shelter's animals to the internet. That exact class of miss has already happened twice in this codebase at a smaller scale: `0101` closed the public gallery and the photo proxy and profile photos still leaked through three other views until `0103`, and #182 gated five route trees while a vet could still write the `vets` table through the API until `0105`. **Not before Lanna is live** — go-live is still gated on the Pi origin, the domain cutover and the AppSheet cutover, and one running reference shelter is what turns seven interested into seven committed. But **pre-production is the cheapest this will ever be**: adding a tenant column when one shelter has data is far cheaper than when seven do. Record the outcome in `docs/decisions.md` whichever way it goes. Note what is being given up: one database means one blast radius, so a bad migration takes all seven down at once where a silo could roll shelter by shelter. **The product needs its own name and domain (Lutan, 2026-09-28).** Once more than one shelter uses it, the app is no longer Lanna's, so it should not live on `lannacare.org` — that stays Lanna's public site, and each shelter keeps its own domain for its own public pages. Choose a name for the application itself and register a matching **`.org`** to host the staff app on (e.g. `app.<name>.org`, with the shelters' domains or subdomains pointing at the same Worker). **The whole project is in honour of Cooper, Lutan's dog who died recently**, so the name should carry him — shortlist a few Cooper-based `.org` names, check which are free (Cloudflare Registrar, where `lannacare.org` already is, sells at cost), and let Lutan choose. *Shortlist checked 2026-09-28 against the .org registry (RDAP), all unregistered that day: cooperscare.org, coopercare.org, coopershaven.org, cooperskeeper.org, coopersheart.org, coopersden.org, cooperspaws.org, friendsofcooper.org, cooperslegacy.org, cooperscircle.org. Already taken: coopercares, coopersfriends, coopersrescue, coopersplace, teamcooper. Re-check at checkout; a registry premium price shows only there.* Register it through Cloudflare so DNS, Email Routing and the Worker routes sit alongside the existing domain. Decide the name before the tenancy build, because it goes into the Worker routes, auth redirect URLs (Supabase and Google OAuth), release mail's sender and the manual. **ONE CONCRETE PER-SHELTER FIELD IS ALREADY KNOWN, 2026-10-09: the receipt issuer.** The donation-receipts item hard-codes the foundation's registered address and (later) tax identifiers, on Lutan's decision that a receipt must not read a field management can edit. That is right for one shelter and **breaks outright for several** — a receipt would carry another shelter's registered address, which is a financial document naming the wrong legal entity. When this spike is scoped, the issuer record (name, address lines, registration and tax identifiers, **per country**) is a worked example of per-shelter configuration that is **Admin-only and audited**, not ordinary settings. The receipts build is required to read it through a single accessor so the swap is contained. Related: *Per-shelter Drive* and *Send all auth mail from one sender domain*, which is already blocked on seven shelters not fitting one sender.

- [ ] **Per-shelter Drive: each shelter keeps its photos in its own Google account.** From the seven-shelter discussion, Lutan 2026-09-28. Do **not** pool the photos even if the database is pooled. Each shelter uses their own Google account — 15GB free each — so storage cost never lands on Lutan and never grows without bound, and the photos live in an account the shelter owns, which matters if they ever leave or the arrangement ends. That makes Drive **per-shelter configuration, not per-shelter infrastructure**: a folder id and OAuth credentials keyed by `shelter_id` rather than the single set of env vars `src/lib/google/drive.ts` reads today. **The risk this creates is the one that has already bitten twice, multiplied by seven.** A Drive refresh token dying breaks that shelter's uploads silently until someone tries to add a photo: on 2026-09-25 the `lanna-care-dev` consent screen was still in *Testing*, so the token expired after 7 days and every upload on lannacare.org failed; a 90-day expiry is set somewhere and still unlocated (see Deployment). With seven shelters this stops being an incident and becomes a recurring support load. **Most of the fix already exists** — `scripts/check-drive-token.mjs`, the Drive-connected indicator on `/admin`, and the status-alert mailer from `0098` (#174). Extend the alerting to check each shelter's token and mail before a shelter notices, and treat that as a **prerequisite of onboarding shelter #2, not a follow-up**. Also decide where per-shelter OAuth credentials live: Worker secrets do not scale to seven, so most likely the database, and then how they are protected. **Spike, 2026-10-09:** `GOOGLE_DRIVE_ROOT_FOLDER_ID` is read in 12 places today. `is_known_drive_file` (the photo proxy’s gate) is one of the definer functions the tenancy build re-owns, so it becomes tenant-scoped once anon carries a shelter, as long as the proxy sends one.

- [ ] **Ask the Chiang Mai five whether they want one regional adoption listing or five separate sites.** From the seven-shelter discussion, Lutan 2026-09-28. This is a product question that decides architecture more firmly than hosting cost does, and it is cheap to ask now and expensive to discover later. Five of the seven interested shelters are in Chiang Mai. Either they want **five separate sites** — each its own brand, adoption page and donors — or they want **one regional network**: a combined "dogs available in Chiang Mai" listing, Shelter Friends shared across shelters, and vet clinics entered once rather than five times (they will largely use the same clinics). The second is the stronger mission outcome — more animals seen by more people — and under a pooled database it is **nearly free to build**, where under a silo it would need a data warehouse on top. If even two of the five want the combined listing, pooling wins outright and the spike above becomes urgent rather than exploratory. Ask before the spike reports, so its answer can shape what the spike measures. Record what they say in `docs/decisions.md`. **Spike, 2026-10-09:** under the chosen design, a combined listing is one deliberate exception: a `postgres`-owned view naming the opted-in shelters, allow-listed by name in the tenancy lint. Still cheap. Shared vet clinics would be a deliberate cross-tenant table; v1 assumes each shelter enters its own, and one login per shelter.

- [x] **Public website photos load slowly: serve sized copies, cached on the Pi, not the originals.** Lutan, 2026-10-01. **Done 2026-10-01** by `claude/public-photo-sizing` (decisions/2026-10-01-public-photo-sizing.md): widths 160/400/1200, Pi disk cache capped at 1 GiB; the phone-from-Thailand timing is Lutan's. Seen on project pages (`/our-work`, `/our-work/[id]`); **scope is every public-facing image** (Lutan, same day): project cards and galleries, resident photos on `/adopt`, `/adopt/[id]`, `/r/` and the home page cards, pet of the week, the hero and site gallery, recent adoptions, adoption updates shown publicly, and Shelter Friend logos. Staff-only photos inside the app stay as they are for now. **Likely cause, from the code:** every image is the full-size original. `driveImageUrl(fileId)` (`src/lib/google/drive-client.ts`) is just `/api/photos/<fileId>` with no size, the photo route streams Drive's `alt=media` bytes as uploaded, and `next.config.ts` sets `images.unoptimized: true`, so `next/image` does no resizing either. A project card (`ProjectCard.tsx`), the story gallery's main image and **every thumbnail in its strip** (`StoryGallery.tsx` → `ThumbnailStrip`) each download a phone-camera original, often 3–10 MB, so a story with twenty photos can be over 100 MB before anyone taps anything. Every other public image uses the same route, so the same fix covers them all. **Measure first** (a real phone, from Thailand): bytes and time for `/our-work` and one story, cold and warm, so the fix can be shown to work. **Fix:** let the photo route take a width (e.g. `/api/photos/<id>?w=400`, only from a small fixed set such as 160 / 400 / 1200 so the cache cannot be flooded with sizes), served from Drive's own rendition through the existing `drive.downloadThumbnail(fileId, size)` (`src/lib/google/drive.ts`, today used only by the deceased-archive PDF), which also turns phone HEIC into JPEG. Fall back to the original if Drive has no rendition yet. **Keep the sized copies on the Pi (Lutan, 2026-10-01):** now that the Pi serves the site, the route writes each generated size to a disk cache on its SSD (e.g. `<cache dir>/<fileId>/<width>.jpg`) and serves it from there next time, so Drive is asked for a given size once rather than on every edge-cache miss. Small files make the Pi's home upload a non-issue for thumbnails and cards. Rules: Cloudflare's edge cache stays in front (the Pi is the origin, not a replacement); only files `is_public_drive_file` approves are written to disk, so internal attachments never land there; the cache is disposable (no backup, safe to empty, size-capped with oldest-first eviction), and Drive stays the source of truth; when a photo is replaced or deleted in the app, its cached sizes are removed (or the cache key includes something that changes, such as Drive's `modifiedTime`). When the Worker is serving without the Pi (fallback), it skips the disk and goes to Drive as today. Cache each size under its own key with the same public/private rules the route already applies (`is_public_drive_file`, `Cache-Control`). Then give `driveImageUrl` a size argument and use it on every public page listed above: thumbnails ~160, cards ~400, the gallery's main image ~1200 with a `srcset`, and a "view original" only where someone actually wants it. Keep `loading="lazy"` off-screen and `priority` only on the first image. Check the edge and Pi caching still apply per size, and that a staff-only photo is still refused when signed out at every size. **This takes in most of the Pi spike below:** it answers the spike's question (2) and builds its pull-through cache, for sized copies. Afterwards the spike only needs to measure whether full-size originals are worth caching on the Pi too. A releases line (visitors and staff will notice faster pages). No schema.

Today `/api/photos/<fileId>` (`src/app/api/photos/[fileId]/route.ts`) fetches a public photo from Drive through the authenticated API and caches it 24 hours at Cloudflare's edge and in the browser; only a cold miss costs a Drive round trip. Under `next start` on the Pi there is no edge Cache API (the route feature-detects it), so the Worker's own caching is what covers repeat views. - [ ] **The Pi is a single point of failure for every write, on both environments, and the Worker fallback only covers reads. DEFERRED 2026-10-19 on priority (see the decided failover programme below) — the risk is unchanged and accepted meanwhile.** Found live on 2026-10-02: the Pi went off the network mid-release and **nobody could sign in or save anything on production**, while every public page still rendered. Three paths confirmed it was the Pi and not name resolution — mDNS (`lanna-pi.local`, `lanna-pi`) silent, the cached LAN address `192.168.68.102` (a Raspberry Pi Foundation MAC) answering neither ping nor port 22, and `POST https://lannacare.org/login` returning `503 x-lanna-served-by: pi-timeout` while `GET` returned 200. The Supabase auth config was checked and was correct, so this was not an auth fault: **"Continue with Google" is a server action, so a POST** — the flow dies before the redirect to Google is issued and the user sees a bare `503` body ("The shelter's server did not answer in time"), which reads as a dead page. Email-and-password sign-in fails identically. **Since this release, test is on the same Pi** (`test-pi.lannacare.org`, same box, same tunnel), so one machine going down now takes writes out on **production and test at once — including the environment you would use to verify a fix.** The cloudflared config anticipates this (`# A second Pi later: run cloudflared there with this same tunnel's credentials and Cloudflare balances between the two`), but there is one Pi. **Three separable pieces, smallest first.** (a) **Distinguish a connect-time failure from an in-flight one in `worker/origin.mjs`.** It splits on method alone — `const idempotent = IDEMPOTENT_METHODS.has(request.method)` — and every failure path returns `idempotent ? null : writeUnanswered()`, so a write is refused whether the Pi timed out mid-request or the fetch never left the Worker. **Keep the refusal where it is right:** a 502/504 can be cloudflared losing the origin *after* the Pi has acted, and replaying would record a second intake (#250, and that file's own comment). But a connection refused or a DNS failure means the request provably never arrived, so replaying locally cannot duplicate anything. Today's outage was entirely the second kind, and **one condition would have meant no outage at all** — writes would have fallen through to the Worker exactly as reads did. Check what the Workers runtime actually surfaces for a connect failure versus a timeout before relying on the distinction; if `fetch` throws indistinguishably, a short pre-flight (a `HEAD` with a one-second timeout, or the status the `scheduled` handler already collects) is the fallback plan. (b) **Nothing said the Pi was down.** It was found because a person could not sign in. Settings → System status has a Pi tile — behind a login that stops working when the Pi does, so the one place that would say so is unreachable exactly when it matters. The Worker stays up in that state and already runs a cron every fifteen minutes (`wrangler.jsonc`, status alerts), so it is the natural place to notice and send the mail `0098` built. (c) **The weekly backup runs on the Pi**, so a Pi down over a Sunday means no backup that week, silently — a larger exposure than the outage. Either run it somewhere that is not the same single point of failure, or alert when a run is missed. **Also worth deciding, separately:** whether emptying `ORIGIN_HOST` should be a documented emergency lever. Setting it to `""` in an environment's block and deploying makes the Worker serve everything including writes, restoring sign-in within a deploy, at the cost of the CPU limits the Pi was adopted to avoid (`Error 1102`). It worked that way until 2026-09-30 and is currently folklore rather than a runbook step. **Status 2026-10-02: (a) is done** (`claude/origin-write-fallback`; docs/decisions/2026-10-02-origin-write-fallback.md). A thrown fetch turned out not to distinguish the two cases — workerd words a refused connect and a connection dropped after the write arrived identically — so the split is on the edge's status instead: a write is rendered by the Worker on a **530** (no tunnel connector, error 1033) and refused as before on everything else. **Status, `claude/pi-down-alert`: (b) is done** — the alert run now treats a dead Pi as red (the tile stays amber), so the existing two-consecutive-runs mail and recovery mail fire for it, with what to check in the body (docs/decisions/2026-10-02-pi-down-alert.md). **Still open: (c) (the existing backup tile alerts only after two missed Sundays; one constant changes that), the `ORIGIN_HOST` lever, and the drill that proves (a) on the real tunnel** (stop `cloudflared` on the Pi, sign in). **Staleness sweep 2026-10-14:** part (c) is closed: #567 (`cae7aba1`) made the backup daily and the tile amber at 2 days, red at 3, so "alerts only after two missed Sundays" no longer holds. Still open: the `ORIGIN_HOST` lever and the tunnel drill. **DEFERRED 2026-10-19 by Lutan, and moved out of Next up:** *"We will push this down the priority list for now so we can finish all the build work first."* **Nothing here is blocked and nothing is undecided** — the options paper is answered (option 1, drills first) and the programme shape is written below. It is parked on priority alone, and it comes back when the feature build work is done. **Do not read this as waiting on anyone, and do not re-ask Lutan the paper’s two questions when it is picked up — they are answered.**
- [ ] **Pi failover: DECIDED 2026-10-19 by Lutan — OPTION 1, make saving safe to repeat, and run the DRILLS FIRST. The paper is answered; this is now a programme to build, not a decision. DEFERRED 2026-10-19 on priority until the feature build work is done.** Lutan, 2026-10-02: not happy with where the write fallback (`claude/origin-write-fallback`, docs/decisions/2026-10-02-origin-write-fallback.md) leaves us. The 2026-10-02 production release notes set it out: **`cloudflared` stopped → 530 at once → writes fall back and work**; **power cut, first seconds → 502/504 or a 20 s timeout → writes refused**; **power cut, once the edge notices → 530 → fall back**; **Pi up but sick, or `lanna-care` stopped → 502/503 from cloudflared → refused**. So the one case that falls back cleanly is the drill, and a power cut (the likeliest outage for a box in a house) starts with a window of refused sign-ins and saves, and a sick-but-up Pi never falls back at all. "If it's not going to fail over properly, we need a different solution." **Why it is built this way, so the replacement keeps the guarantee:** a 502/504 can arrive *after* the Pi has written, so replaying it on the Worker could record a second intake (#250), and a thrown fetch cannot tell "never arrived" from "arrived, then dropped" (the decision file's probe table). Any new design must still never apply a write twice. **The key fact to build on: the data is not on the Pi.** Both the Pi and the Worker write to the same Supabase database, so the duplicate risk can be closed *at the database* rather than by guessing at the edge, after which retrying on the Worker is always safe. **Options to weigh, not mutually exclusive:** (1) **Idempotent writes.** Every server action carries a client-generated request id, and the database records it under a unique key in the same transaction as the write (one shared wrapper around `runAction()` plus a `write_requests` table, or a parameter on the RPCs that matter: intake, placements, weights, deliveries, stocktake, uploads' attachment rows). A replay then returns the first result instead of writing again, and **every** failure (502, 504, timeout, thrown fetch) can fall back to the Worker. It removes the "refused by design" rows outright, but it touches every write path, so it needs its own schema PR and a sweep like #441's. (2) **Route on health, not on each request's outcome.** The Pi sends a heartbeat every few seconds (or the Worker's cron probes it) into Workers KV or a Durable Object; when it is stale the Worker serves *everything* itself before trying the Pi, so a new request after a power cut never waits for the edge to notice. Covers the "Pi up but sick" row too if the heartbeat comes from the app rather than the OS. It does not cover a request already in flight when the power goes, which is what (1) is for. (3) **Keep the power on.** A UPS HAT or small UPS for the Pi *and* the router/ONT (the tunnel needs both), sized for a typical Suphan Buri outage, with a clean shutdown on low battery. Cheapest and most direct for the power-cut row; does nothing for a crash or a broken deploy. (4) **A second connector on the same tunnel**, off-site: cloudflared already supports replicas ("A second Pi later" in `scripts/pi/cloudflared-config.yml`), and a free-tier cloud VM (e.g. an always-free ARM instance) running the same build would keep the origin up when the house goes dark. Real redundancy at near-zero cost, but a second machine to deploy to, patch and keep the secrets on, and each replica serves a share of traffic, not only the failover. (5) **Flip it: writes always on the Worker, the Pi only for page renders.** The 1102s came from rendering, not from server actions, so writes might fit the Worker's CPU budget. Then a Pi outage costs reads (which already fall back) and never writes. It hinges on a Pi-rendered form posting to a Worker build, which needs the same server-action ids and a shared `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (the open Deployment item), so verify that first. Paid Cloudflare Load Balancing was considered and is out: it costs every month and cannot target a Worker. **Deliverable:** a short paper (`docs/pi-failover.md`) that measures before it argues: on the real tunnel, time how long a hard power-off takes to become a 530 (pull the plug, POST every second), and what a stopped `lanna-care` returns. Then a recommendation of the cheapest combination that makes every row of the table "falls back and works" without ever risking a double write. My expectation is (1) + (2), with (3) as cheap insurance, but let the measurements decide. Agree it with Lutan, record it in `docs/decisions/`, then build (schema PR first if (1)). **Done when** the drill passes for all four rows: stop `cloudflared`, pull the power, stop `lanna-care`, and wedge the app, and in each case a sign-in and a save made during the outage succeed exactly once. Supersedes the `ORIGIN_HOST=""` emergency-lever question in the item above if (2) lands, and pairs with that item's (b), the alert when the Pi goes down. **Status 2026-10-03: the options paper is written and proposed ([#310](https://github.com/lutanbennett/Animal_Shelter_App/pull/310), `docs/pi-failover.md`); it is not agreed and no drill has been run. Remaining: Lutan reads it and answers its two questions; the drill (recipe in the paper) is run on the Pi; option 5 waits only on a CPU measurement (the form-key question is answered: a shared key is required and works on both the Pi’s and the Worker’s build, per `server-actions-encryption-key`, 2026-10-03, and it is live only once #312 is merged and both builds are redeployed); then the agreed recommendation goes in `docs/decisions/` and the build is planned.** **Architecture review, 2026-10-11 (`docs/architecture-review-2026-09-22.md`):** an outside reader's view for the decision, not a new item. The Worker render fallback is the expensive half of the asymmetry: it is why there are two builds per release, why the shared Server Actions key exists, why writes are cloned into Worker memory, why `strip-baked-env.mjs` exists, and where three of the four live faults since 2026-09-30 arose. What it buys is anonymous public pages (which the edge cache already covers) and degraded staff *reads* under the 10 ms CPU limit; writes under it are refused in every outage shape but a stopped `cloudflared`. So the honest alternatives are (a) keep it and make writes idempotent (option 1 of the paper, weeks), or (b) drop the fallback for app paths — the Worker becomes cache + proxy and app routes get a static "back shortly" page during an outage — which removes the dual-build class of fault for a few lines in `worker/index.mjs` and `origin.mjs` and the deletion of the actions-key machinery. Run the paper's drills first; they say whether the reads (b) gives up were worth anything. Review §2.2 C1. **DECIDED 2026-10-19 (Lutan), both questions on the last page of `docs/pi-failover.md`:** (1) *"I want to go for option 1 - the bigger build but proper fix. Let’s do it right the first time."* So **a refused window is NOT acceptable and must be zero**, which the paper says only option 1 delivers. (2) *"And yes do the drills first."* **This supersedes the paper’s own recommendation**, which was to do options 3 and 2 first and hold 1 until the leftover window had been measured — Lutan has chosen the end state directly rather than approaching it in cheap steps. **Do not re-litigate it, and do not quietly substitute options 2 and 3 because they are cheaper.** **WHAT THIS IS: a programme of several streams, not a workstream.** The paper is explicit — *"it touches every place the app saves (intake, placements, weights, deliveries, stocktake, attachments) … weeks, several streams"*. **Briefing it as one stream would produce an unfinishable session** (see the 2026-10-18 acceptance dry run, which reached 819,980 tokens at ~35% done and had to be stopped). Plan it as: **(A) the drills and measurements** — no code, no schema; **(B) a schema PR** for the ticket table and the record-in-the-same-step guarantee; **(C) the shared wrapper** every save goes through; then **(D) the sweep**, split by area into finishable streams the way #441’s sweep was, one group of save sites each. **Each sweep stream names the save sites it owns and stops there.** **(A) THE DRILLS MUST ALSO SETTLE OPTION 5, and this is the cheapest thing on the whole item.** The paper says option 5 (the Worker does all the saving, the Pi only draws pages) *"may make all of the above unnecessary for saving"* and is blocked on **one unmeasured number: whether saving fits the Worker’s CPU limit**. The form-key question it also waited on was answered on 2026-10-03. **So take that measurement in the drill stream, before any of (B), (C) or (D) starts.** If saving fits on the Worker, several weeks of sweep may be avoidable, and that is worth one measurement. **This is not a reason to delay the decision — Lutan has made it — but measuring before building is what he asked for, and this is the measurement with the largest consequence.** Report the number to him either way and say plainly what it does or does not change. **Option 3 (a battery for the Pi, the router and the fibre box) stays worth doing and is NOT superseded by option 1.** Option 1 makes a failed save safe to retry; it does not keep the Pi answering, and page-drawing still degrades to the Worker during an outage. It is a one-off hardware purchase with no code, and it needs the one fact the paper says nobody has written down: **how long recent Suphan Buri outages actually lasted.** Keep it as its own item rather than folding it into the programme. **The decision file is owed and CANNOT be written from the `backlog` branch:** `docs/decisions/2026-10-02-pi-failover.md`, which `docs/pi-failover.md` names as the place the agreed recommendation is recorded. **It goes in the FIRST PR of the programme (the drill stream), carrying Lutan’s two answers verbatim and the drill numbers**, so the reasoning is on `main` before any build depends on it. **DEFERRED 2026-10-19 by Lutan, and moved out of Next up:** *"We will push this down the priority list for now so we can finish all the build work first."* **Nothing here is blocked and nothing is undecided** — the options paper is answered (option 1, drills first) and the programme shape is written below. It is parked on priority alone, and it comes back when the feature build work is done. **Do not read this as waiting on anyone, and do not re-ask Lutan the paper’s two questions when it is picked up — they are answered.**

- [ ] **The 15 GB Drive figure is wrong in a decision file on `main`, and the backup retention was partly sized against it (small PR).** Found 2026-10-19, after Lutan confirmed the shelter's account `lannacareforanimals@gmail.com` holds **1 TB**, not the free 15 GB that several items assumed. **The backlog is now corrected; `docs/decisions/2026-10-12-daily-backup-prune-by-age.md` is not**, and it still reasons from “the shelter's 15 GB” (line 44). A decision file that argues from a wrong number is worse than a stale backlog item, because it is the thing a future session reads to avoid re-deriving the answer. **Do:** correct the figure in that decision file, say which account it refers to (the backups land on the `lannaanimalfoundationbwm` tree today, not the shelter's, so **check that account's quota before writing a number** rather than assuming 1 TB applies there too), and add a line saying what the corrected figure does and does not change. **It does NOT automatically justify keeping more backups.** The two-week retention is also a privacy choice, and a dump holds medical history and names carers and adopters — if the retention changes, that is its own decision with Lutan, not a consequence of having more disk. **Also check** whether any other sizing argument in the repo rests on 15 GB (`grep -rn "15 GB" docs/ src/`).
- [ ] **When a decision is answered, change the item’s TITLE and mark the superseded text — appending the answer at the bottom is not enough (small PR to `CLAUDE.md`).** Filed 2026-10-19 by Lutan, after being asked for the third time for a decision he had already given twice. **The decisions were never missing from the backlog.** Each was recorded, accurately, at the *end* of a very long item — while the item’s title still said “decision first” and the superseded reasoning still sat in the middle reading as live. Three instances in one day: the Pi OOM item still asked for a peak-memory measurement under a title saying BLOCKING when the real cause had been found; the videos item still said “decision on storage first” and “15 GB free” when the answer (1 TB, store in Drive) was in its own last paragraph; the vet-calendar item still said “settle whether it is configured” when that had been answered on 2026-10-17. **Why it bites: anything that reads the backlog quickly reads the title.** A planner, a checklist, a `/plan-day` run and a person skimming all do. An item whose title lies costs the user the same decision twice and makes the record look untrustworthy when it is not. **Do:** add a rule to `CLAUDE.md` — when a stream or a chat records an answer on an item, it must (1) rewrite the title so the title alone says what is still open, (2) mark the superseded passage in place rather than leaving it to be read as current, and (3) say plainly if nothing is left to decide. Consider a cheap checker: an open item whose body contains `ANSWERED`/`DECIDED` *and* whose title contains “decide”, “decision first” or “settle” is almost certainly stale — a scan on 2026-10-19 flagged five, of which three were genuinely stale. **Not a `backlog`-branch edit: `CLAUDE.md` changes go through a PR.**

Concretely it does **not** contain the `public_impact_figures` allowlist entry from #420, so `public-views` will fail on it the moment anything triggers a run, for a reason that has nothing to do with bumping action versions. **Why it matters more than one stale PR:** a red check on a dependency PR is how a security update gets ignored, and 2026-10-07 already showed what a red check nobody can explain costs — the release manager lost 45 minutes to one. **What to do:** rebase it on `main` (or comment `@dependabot rebase`), see whether CI is then genuinely green, and either merge it or close it with a reason. The actions in `.github/workflows/` are currently pinned by SHA with a version comment, so check what the bump actually changes and keep the pinning style. If it is closed rather than merged, say why here, because Dependabot will raise it again. → *Documentation* **Done 2026-10-07 (`claude/dependabot-264`):** the bump (`actions/checkout` v4 → v7.0.1, `actions/setup-node` v4 → v7.0.0, still pinned by SHA, both SHAs checked against the upstream tags) is carried on this branch with a test plan, and #264 is closed as superseded: Dependabot closes its own PR once `main` has the new versions. The item's prediction was wrong. PR CI runs on the merge commit with `main`, so #264's age never mattered and `public-views` passed. The only red was `test-plan`, because a bot PR cannot carry a plan, and every future Dependabot PR will hit the same thing. See `docs/decisions/2026-10-07-dependabot-prs-carried-on-a-branch.md`.

- [x] **Clickable links in the text of the website's pages (e.g. DonorBox on Donate).** Lutan, 2026-10-04. The shelter takes donations through **DonorBox** (donorbox.org) among other methods, and the Donate page's text names the DonorBox address, but it shows as plain text a visitor has to copy into the address bar. On a phone, which is how most visitors arrive, that usually means they don't. **Why it happens:** page bodies typed on Settings → Website are rendered by `SiteBody` (`src/components/SiteBody.tsx`) through `parseBody()` (`src/lib/site/body.ts`), which understands paragraphs, `## ` sub-headings and `- ` bullet lists only. Everything else, a URL included, is printed as text. **Build:** (1) **Bare URLs become links on their own.** Any `https://…` or `www.…` in a body is linked, so what is already typed (the DonorBox address) starts working without anyone re-editing it. Strip trailing punctuation the way a reader expects ("…donorbox.org/lanna." links without the full stop). (2) **Links with words**, so the page can say "Give monthly on DonorBox" rather than show the raw address. Use Markdown's `[Give monthly on DonorBox](https://donorbox.org/…)`, since `parseBody` already borrows Markdown's `## ` and `- `. Also allow an email address (`mailto:`) and a phone number (`tel:`), which are just as useful on a phone. (3) **Safe by construction:** build the link as a React element from the parsed parts, never as HTML from the text; accept only `https:`, `http:`, `mailto:`, `tel:` and paths on this site (`/adopt`, `/friends/join`), and print anything else (`javascript:`, `data:`) as plain text. A link to another site opens in a new tab with `rel="noopener noreferrer"` and a visible "opens in a new tab" cue for screen readers. Style it so it reads as a link on the cream background, with enough contrast in both themes and a tap target of at least 44 px on a phone. (4) **Everywhere `SiteBody` is used:** the information pages (Donate, Foster, Volunteer, How to adopt, International adoption, Become a Shelter Friend) and the home page's story, so one change covers them all. Decide while building whether the same rule should reach other public text that staff type: project stories on `/our-work/[id]`, resident bios on `/adopt/[id]` and Shelter Friend blurbs. Probably yes for project stories and friends, which are where an outside link is natural, but check each renderer and say which in the decision file. (5) **Translations:** a Thai version goes through the translation queue, so a translator must keep the address part of `[…](…)` unchanged. Say so in the translation editor's hint, and have the translation check refuse a Thai version whose links differ from the English. (6) **The editor:** a one-line hint under each body field on Settings → Website ("Paste a web address and it becomes a link. For your own words: [words](https://…)"), and a preview that shows the link working before Save. **Also, separately and worth asking:** a proper **Donate on DonorBox** button on `/donate` (and perhaps the header's Donate button pointing there), with the address as a Website setting rather than typed in the text, so the most important donation link is a big button and not a line in a paragraph. That overlaps the Fundraising items ("Make `/donate` ask for money", the per-donation QR paper), which should mention DonorBox now that the shelter is known to use it. No schema for the links themselves. Manual (the Website topic), both dictionaries for the hints, a decision file, a releases line (visitors will notice links that work), and a test plan covering a bare link, a worded link, an email, a phone number, a refused `javascript:` link and a Thai page.

- [ ] **Google Search Console: three indexing complaints, all expected while the site is locked — settle them as part of go-live, not before.** Lutan, 2026-10-07, who flagged them himself and said plainly *"not an issue yet while we are still developing"*. Search Console reports **Blocked by robots.txt**, **Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt**, and **Duplicate without user-selected canonical**. **The first two are the app working as designed, and should NOT be "fixed" now.** `src/app/robots.ts` is deliberately dynamic (`force-dynamic`, because `PUBLIC_SITE` is a Worker var read per request) and returns `disallow: /` for every agent while the public site is locked, which is the state production ships in until go-live; the proxy's `X-Robots-Tag` says the same on every response. So "blocked by robots.txt" is the correct answer to Google today. *Indexed, though blocked* is Google having reached a URL by a link and indexed it without being able to crawl it — robots.txt stops crawling, not indexing. Unlocking is what clears both, and that is a go-live step with its own gate (`scripts/deploy.mjs` refuses `--env production` while the block is off `lannacare.org` and still locked). **The third one is a real gap and the only thing to build here.** No page sets `alternates.canonical`: the public pages set `metadataBase` from `getSiteOrigin()` and nothing more (`src/app/page.tsx`, `adopt/`, `adopt/[id]/`, `our-work/[id]/`, `friends/`, `privacy/`, `e/[id]/`, `r/[code]/`). With the same content reachable on more than one host or path, Google picks its own canonical and says so. **So, at go-live:** add an explicit `alternates: { canonical }` to each public page's metadata, built from the same `getSiteOrigin()` the `metadataBase` already uses, so the canonical always names `lannacare.org` and never the test host or the Pi origin. **Check while doing it:** that `test.lannacare.org` and the Pi origin stay `noindex` (they are locked, and `e/[id]`, `r/[code]`, `no-access` and the locked landing are individually `robots: { index: false }` already), that the canonical survives the Worker/Pi split, and whether a sitemap is wanted — `robots.ts` names none today. **Then re-request indexing in Search Console**, since these three will not clear on their own once the cause is gone. **Do not touch `robots.ts`'s locked branch** to make Search Console quieter before go-live: a crawlable pre-launch site is the thing that behaviour exists to prevent. → *Public website* **Note 2026-10-14 (`claude/public-site-findability`):** the "whether a sitemap is wanted" question above is answered — `src/app/sitemap.ts` exists and `robots.ts` names it once unlocked. The three complaints are still possible: the first two clear only with unlocking, and no page sets `alternates.canonical` yet. Still go-live work. **Note 2026-10-14 (`claude/seo-audit-fable`):** the canonical half is built — every public page now sets `alternates.canonical` from `getSiteOrigin()`, the bare path, so the third complaint clears once Google re-crawls. **And a correction: the public site opens on `lannacareforanimals.org`, not `lannacare.org`** (decided 2026-10-10), so the Search Console property to verify and submit the sitemap to is `lannacareforanimals.org` (a *Domain* property, TXT record in Cloudflare DNS); the `lannacare.org` property keeps the staff app, which stays `noindex`. What is left is exactly the go-live-day sequence in the cutover item: unlock, check robots.txt and the sitemap on the new host, verify the property, submit the sitemap, request indexing of the home page and one animal, and re-request indexing of the three complained-about URLs.

- [ ] **A unique QR code per donation that records itself and links to the donor, the way TrueMoney and Lazada top-ups do — options paper first, then build.** Lutan, 2026-10-02. **How those apps do it:** each top-up gets its own **dynamic** Thai QR carrying the amount and a reference; when the payer's bank app pays it, the payment provider tells the merchant's system (a webhook), and the reference says exactly which order it was. A plain PromptPay QR (to a phone number or tax ID) has neither: no reference, and nothing tells the system the money arrived, so a donation can only be matched later from a bank statement. This item is that automatic path, and it builds on "Make `/donate` ask for money and record what arrives" just above (its step (b) `donations` table is the record this fills in; its step (d) named a hosted gateway). **The three ways to get there, for the paper to compare honestly:** (1) **a payment gateway** that issues a PromptPay QR per payment and sends a webhook when it is paid (Opn Payments, formerly Omise, which the `/donate` item already names; GB Prime Pay and 2C2P are other Thai options): least paperwork and quickest to build, at a per-transaction fee; (2) **the shelter's own bank** offering Thai QR bill payment with reference fields and a payment notification API (most Thai banks offer a corporate version): no middleman, but it needs a corporate account set up for it, a biller ID and the bank's onboarding; (3) **no integration**: a static PromptPay QR plus importing the bank statement and matching by amount and time, the fallback when (1) and (2) are not available, and fragile (two people giving 500 baht the same morning). For each, record: fees, what the foundation must provide to sign up (registration documents, a juristic-person account), settlement time, sandbox/test mode, and whether overseas donors can pay too (cards, which PromptPay does not cover). **Shape once chosen:** `/donate` (and a "sponsor {name}" button on a resident, and an appeal's page once those exist) asks for an amount, and optionally a name and contact for a receipt, then shows a QR made for that donation with a short reference and a countdown; the page turns to "Thank you, received" when the webhook arrives. The webhook route (`src/app/api/...`) verifies the provider's signature, is idempotent (the same notification twice records one donation), records the amount the **provider** confirms (never the amount the page asked for), and links the row to the donation it was created for: the donor's contact if they gave one, a resident or appeal if designated. Anonymous giving stays possible. Staff see it on Management → Donations from the `/donate` item. **Linking to the person:** a donor who leaves a name and contact becomes (or is matched to) a `contacts` row, by email or phone, with their consent recorded, so repeat donors build up a history; nothing personal is asked for to make a donation. **Tax receipts:** check whether the foundation is registered for the Revenue Department's e-Donation system; if donors want a tax deduction it may need their Thai ID number, which is sensitive personal data (PDPA), so collect it only when they ask for a receipt, store it apart and decide retention in the paper. **Must hold:** no card or bank details ever touch the app or the Pi; the webhook must be reachable even if the Pi is down (the Worker fallback answers it, and providers retry); keys are Worker secrets; money goes straight to the shelter's own account, never through the platform, which also keeps each shelter separate when there are several. **Deliverable:** `docs/donations-payments.md` comparing the options with real fees and sign-up requirements, a `docs/decisions/` entry once Lutan and the Director choose, then the build (schema PR first) in the provider's test mode end to end before any real money.
